old_row.relationship: Children dashed in judgment against Babylon
old_row.rationale: The psalm’s violent blessing concerning Babylon’s infants corresponds to Isaiah’s Babylon oracle describing their children dashed before them. Isaiah does not specify the psalm’s rock, and the comparison reports the texts rather than extending their command to another setting.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Children dashed in judgment against Babylon
proposed_new_row.rationale: The psalm’s violent blessing concerning Babylon’s infants corresponds to Isaiah’s Babylon oracle describing their children dashed before them. Isaiah does not specify the psalm’s rock.

proposed_changes.reason: The source is a blessing and the target is a prediction; neither retained unit issues the command claimed by the deleted clause.

old_row.relationship: Preservation amid affliction and hostile power
old_row.rationale: The speaker’s life is preserved amid affliction and enemies’ anger; Psalm 17 describes enemies overtaking him on the day of affliction and the Lord becoming his support and rescuer. The right-hand wording belongs to Psalm 137, not the selected target.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Preservation amid affliction and hostile power
proposed_new_row.rationale: Psalm 137 anticipates being kept alive if the speaker walks amid affliction and recalls God stretching His hand against the enemies’ anger and saving him with His right hand. Psalm 17 joins enemies overtaking him on the day of affliction with the Lord becoming his support, bringing him into a spacious place and promising rescue. The conditional expectation and remembered acts remain distinct; the right-hand image belongs to Psalm 137.

proposed_changes.reason: Preserve the source conditional and future life-preservation separately from its completed hand action.

old_row.rationale: Both passages combine divine holding and guidance. Psalm 138 says God’s right hand holds the speaker; Psalm 72 says God grasped the speaker’s right hand and guided him in counsel.

proposed_new_row.rationale: Both passages combine divine holding and guidance. Psalm 138 says God’s right hand will hold the speaker; Psalm 72 says God grasped the speaker’s right hand and guided him in counsel.

proposed_changes.reason: Preserve the source future while distinguishing the target past grasping and guidance.

old_row.relationship: Goliath’s challenge in the named heading
old_row.rationale: The source heading explicitly concerns Goliath; Samuel names Goliath and records his challenge to Israel for single combat. This identifies the named narrative figure without requiring every poetic battle image to be a literal detail of the encounter.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Goliath’s challenge in the named heading
proposed_new_row.rationale: The source heading explicitly concerns Goliath; the account in 1 Samuel names Goliath and records his challenge to Israel for single combat. This identifies the named narrative figure without requiring every poetic battle image to be a literal detail of the encounter.

proposed_changes.reason: Use the account’s book title unambiguously, consistently with the candidate wording correction, without implying personal narrative authorship by Samuel.

old_row.relationship: Speaking of fearsome works and divine power
old_row.rationale: The declaration of God’s fearsome acts and greatness corresponds to the instruction to say to God how fearsome His works are, through the abundance of His power. The target’s enemies lying is not extended to the source.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Speaking of fearsome works and divine power
proposed_new_row.rationale: Psalm 144 anticipates speech about the power of God’s fearsome acts and His greatness. Psalm 65 commands speech to God calling His works fearsome, then says His enemies will lie to Him through the abundance of His power. The fearsome-works and power language is shared, while the target’s consequence for enemies is distinct.

proposed_changes.reason: The through-the-abundance-of-power clause modifies the enemies lying, not the preceding fearsome-works exclamation.

old_row.relationship: Goodness and beauty in the summons to praise
old_row.rationale: Psalm 146 commends praise because a psalm is good and asks that praise please God; Psalm 134 commands praise because the Lord is good and music because His name is beautiful. The differing subjects of good are preserved.

proposed_new_row.relationship: A praise summons with differing goodness clauses
proposed_new_row.rationale: Both summon praise of the Lord and follow it with a goodness clause. Psalm 146 calls a psalm good and asks that praise please God; Psalm 134 calls the Lord good and commands music to His name, adding “for it is beautiful.” The repeated form is compared without equating the subjects of good or resolving the final it.

proposed_changes.reason: Keep the particular repeated praise-and-reason form while preserving different goodness predicates and the supplied final pronoun.

old_row.relationship: Divine breath or wind controls frost and water
old_row.rationale: The Lord’s sending His word to melt the ice and blowing wind so waters flow correspond to frost given from the Strong One’s breath and His steering water as He wishes. Frost-giving and melting are different actions.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Divine breath or wind controls frost and water
proposed_new_row.rationale: Psalm 147 says God will send His word and melt them, blow His wind, and waters will flow. Elihu says frost will be given from the Strong One’s breath and He steers water as He wishes. Divine wind or breath and control of water connect the passages, while frost-giving and melting remain different actions.

proposed_changes.reason: Retain B’s verified Elihu attribution, the stated future wording and the source’s plural object without narrowing it unnecessarily.

old_row.relationship: Creation endures under God’s established word
old_row.rationale: The enduring establishment and command that will not pass away correspond to God’s word remaining in heaven, the founded earth remaining, and all things serving His arrangement. The exact subjects and time expressions remain distinct.

proposed_new_row.relationship: Creation endures under God’s established word
proposed_new_row.rationale: The enduring establishment and command that will not pass away correspond to God’s word remaining in heaven, the founded earth remaining, and the day remaining by His arrangement. The exact subjects and time expressions remain distinct.

proposed_changes.reason: Psalm 118:91 says the day remains by God’s arrangement and all things are His servants; it does not make arrangement the object served.
